I'll evaluate the committed Platform optimization subsystem at the pinned commit. Let me start by exploring the tree structure.The second file (evidence.go) output seems to have been merged. Let me read evidence.go separately and the remaining files.Now the platform registry and the referenced scripts/docs.Now let me examine the tests and referenced docs, plus check a few suspected issues more closely.Now let me examine the test files to understand coverage, and check specific suspected defects.Now let me examine the remaining tests and check a few suspected issues. Let me verify whether the tests actually compile and pass at this commit, and probe some edge cases.Let me verify whether the test suite actually passes at this commit. Let me check if Go is available and run the tests read-only in a temp GOPATH.The test run is slow (module downloads). Let me wait for it.All tests pass at the pinned commit. Now let me examine remaining test files and probe specific suspected defects.Now I have a comprehensive view. Let me probe a few suspected defects with actual code execution against the pinned tree. Let me test specific edge cases.Now let me probe the scheduler cost-optimization tie-breaking logic, which I suspect has a defect, and the solver's cost tie-break interaction.Let me probe more carefully identified concerns: the `validate` makespanUnit inconsistency (empty unit allowed but only "seconds" honored), the `CostModel` validation when no costs present, and the `VerifyRecommendation`/`MeasureScheduleAccuracy` checks. Also the acquisition `satisfies` freshness semantics and the `MeasureCostAccuracy` estimate-vs-realized completeness.Confirmed several hypotheses. Let me probe a few more: the `AssessValue` alternative with an estimate for a criterion but `LifecycleCost` used in policy scoring — and check whether `AssessValuePolicies` errors when a Pareto alternative lacks an estimate for a criterion (can't happen since Pareto membership requires all criteria). Also the `MeancostAccuracy` and DORA half-open window edge. Let me also verify the `build-evaluator-snapshot.sh` git archive determinism claim and the `record-value` empty StoreDirectory behavior.Confirmed: `fmt.Sprint` on `[]string` is not injective, so the alternative-identity guard in `AssessValueScenarios` can be bypassed. The same `fmt.Sprint` pattern is used in `value_policy.go` for selection-change detection. Let me confirm the policy one and also check the `record-value` empty-directory path and main.go's `RecommendationSnapshot` wiring.Now let me verify the `build-evaluator-snapshot.sh` snapshot binding. The commit message says "bind evaluator reviews to git snapshots". A key question: does the EvaluatorRun `InputSnapshotID` (a `snap_<sha256-of-archive>`) actually get cross-checked against the snapshot receipt produced by this script? Let me check whether there's any verification that a run's snapshot ID corresponds to a real commit, and whether the script's `git archive` is deterministic.Key observation: `build-evaluator-snapshot.sh` produces `snap_<sha256 of tar archive>`, but `VerifyEvaluatorRun`/`NewEvaluatorRun` only check `validContentID(InputSnapshotID, "snap_")` — i.e., format only. Nothing in the Go code recomputes the archive digest or links a run's `InputSnapshotID` to a real commit/receipt. The binding is purely by-convention, not executable. Let me verify this gap and check the tar determinism concern.

Let me also verify the snapshot script's `git archive` includes the script itself deterministically and check the git-archive SHA stability across invocations.The archive digest matches the stated `snap_cf8ecd...` and is deterministic across invocations. Now let me confirm the critical gap: the snapshot script validates the *secret scan* on the live tree but nothing ties an `EvaluatorRun` to a verified snapshot receipt in code. Let me also check `main_test.go` and verify the `git archive` exclusion correctness (the script excludes itself from the secret scan but NOT from the archive — fine). Let me look at the remaining test files for coverage gaps.I now have a thorough picture. Let me do a final check on a couple of remaining concerns: the `record-evaluators`/`assess-evaluators` path when `StoreDirectory` is empty for `record-evaluators` (it would attempt Save to "" and error — acceptable fail-closed), and the `VerifyEvaluatorRun` receipt digest semantics. Let me also verify the `git archive` excludes the secret-scan self-exclusion is correct and that the snapshot receipt's `secretScanRevision` is bound to runs. Let me confirm the most important gap precisely: nothing in Go validates that an `EvaluatorRun.InputSnapshotID` corresponds to a receipt produced by `build-evaluator-snapshot.sh`.

Let me verify the cost tie-break direction issue more rigorously — whether a *known* cost can displace an *unknown* cost on an equal load, and whether that can change the makespan outcome vs. documented "cost breaks ties only after the makespan objective."I have enough evidence. Let me clean up the probe file from the extracted tree (not the repo) and finalize my findings.All tests pass at the pinned commit (`ok internal/optimization`, `ok cmd/platform-optimizer`), and the `git archive` digest is deterministic and matches the stated snapshot ID. I evaluated the committed source by reading it and by running executable probes against a clean extraction of the pinned commit. Below are the hypothesis findings.

{"findings":[
{"localId":"F1","clusterKey":"scenario-policy-identity-fmt-sprint-collision","category":"correctness","target":"platform/internal/optimization/value_scenario.go:49","summary":"Alternative-inventory change detection compares `fmt.Sprint(ids)` where ids is a sorted []string; because fmt.Sprint is not injective (e.g. [\"a\",\"b\"] and [\"a b\"] both render as \"[a b]\"), two scenarios with genuinely different alternative identities can be treated as identical, silently bypassing the inventory-change guard the doc promises.","confidence":"9/10","evidence":["value_scenario.go builds `encodedIDs := fmt.Sprint(ids)` and compares strings; an executable probe (scenario1 alternatives [\"a\",\"b\"], scenario2 [\"a b\"]) returned nil error, confirming the guard was bypassed","go test ./internal/optimization with a probe constructing colliding ID sets shows AssessValueScenarios does not reject the identity change"]},
{"localId":"F2","clusterKey":"scenario-policy-identity-fmt-sprint-collision","category":"correctness","target":"platform/internal/optimization/value_policy.go:88","summary":"Policy selection-change detection uses `fmt.Sprint(policyResult.Selected)` as the comparison key; the same non-injective rendering means two different Selected sets can compare equal when an alternative ID contains a space, so SelectionChanges can be falsely reported as false.","confidence":"8/10","evidence":["value_policy.go sets `selection := fmt.Sprint(policyResult.Selected)` and compares to firstSelection; fmt.Sprint on []string is not injective for space-bearing IDs","same root cause as value_scenario.go; a crafted ID set renders distinct selections identically"]},
{"localId":"F3","clusterKey":"twin-fact-value-byte-sensitivity","category":"correctness","target":"platform/internal/optimization/twin.go:131","summary":"BuildTwinSnapshot detects conflicting facts by comparing `string(fact.Value) != string(field.Value)` (raw bytes after json.Compact, which preserves key order), so two semantically identical JSON values with different key order are reported as CONFLICTING rather than KNOWN.","confidence":"9/10","evidence":["probe: two facts with values {\"x\":1,\"y\":2} and {\"y\":2,\"x\":1} for the same requirement produced Status CONFLICTING, though the values are semantically equal","json.Compact in NewTemporalFact does not canonicalize object key order, so conflict detection is byte-order sensitive"]},
{"localId":"F4","clusterKey":"twin-fact-value-byte-sensitivity","category":"correctness","target":"platform/internal/optimization/twin.go:289","summary":"NewTemporalFact derives the content-addressed fact ID from the marshaled struct including the byte-exact Value, so semantically equal facts with different JSON key order yield different fact IDs, fragmenting identity for identical observations.","confidence":"9/10","evidence":["probe: NewTemporalFact on the same logical value with keys in two orders produced id1 != id2","fact identity is byte-sensitive, not value-canonical (no JCS/canonical JSON normalization of Value)"]},
{"localId":"F5","clusterKey":"costmodel-validation-skipped-when-no-item-costs","category":"correctness","target":"platform/internal/optimization/scheduler.go:191","summary":"When a Problem supplies a CostModel but no item carries EstimatedCostMicros (hasCosts==false), validate() skips CostModel currency/source/asOf checks entirely, so a malformed CostModel (bad currency, empty source, non-RFC3339 asOf) is accepted and echoed into Result.CostModel.","confidence":"8/10","evidence":["validate() only enforces CostModel fields inside `if hasCosts {...}`; a probe with CostModel{Currency:\"bad\",Source:\"\",AsOf:\"not-a-time\"} and costless items returned err=nil and the malformed CostModel in the Result","the Result then carries an unvalidated cost model that downstream cost-evidence checks (MeasureCostAccuracy) never re-validate for well-formedness"]},
{"localId":"F6","clusterKey":"cost-tiebreak-treats-unknown-as-worst","category":"documentation","target":"platform/internal/optimization/scheduler.go:300","summary":"On an exact load tie with optimizeCost enabled, a candidate with a KNOWN cost is preferred over one whose cost is UNKNOWN (`cheaper := optimizeCost && candidateKnown && (!bestKnown || ...)`), so a missing estimate is effectively treated as worst-case for placement even though the doc states only that a missing estimate 'suppresses aggregate cost' and is 'not treated as free'; the tie-break direction is undocumented.","confidence":"6/10","evidence":["round() sets cheaper true when candidateKnown && !bestKnown; a probe with one known-cost and one unknown-cost equal-capacity resource assigned the item to the known-cost resource on the tie","ADVISORY-OPTIMIZATION.md says 'a missing estimate remains unknown and suppresses aggregate cost instead of being treated as free' but does not state that unknown cost loses ties to any known cost"]},
{"localId":"F7","clusterKey":"evaluator-snapshot-binding-not-executable","category":"provenance","target":"platform/internal/optimization/evaluator.go:174","summary":"The binding between an EvaluatorRun and the immutable git snapshot is only format-checked: validateEvaluatorRun requires InputSnapshotID to match `snap_`+64-hex, but no code recomputes the platform/ archive digest or cross-checks it against a receipt produced by build-evaluator-snapshot.sh, so a run can claim any well-formed snap_ ID that does not correspond to the audited commit.","confidence":"7/10","evidence":["validateEvaluatorRun calls only validContentID(run.InputSnapshotID, \"snap_\") (length/prefix/hex), never hashing the tree or comparing to build-evaluator-snapshot.sh output","build-evaluator-snapshot.sh emits snap_<sha256-of-tar>, but there is no executable gate linking a recorded EvaluatorRun.InputSnapshotID to that receipt; git grep shows InputSnapshotID is only ever format-validated"]},
{"localId":"F8","clusterKey":"dora-window-duration-overflow-saturation","category":"correctness","target":"platform/internal/optimization/dora.go:52","summary":"AssessDORA computes windowDuration = windowEnd.Sub(windowStart) and later uses windowDuration.Nanoseconds() as a big.Rat denominator and WindowSeconds; for windows approaching/exceeding the int64 duration range (~292 years) time.Time.Sub saturates and Nanoseconds() can overflow, so WindowSeconds/DeploymentFrequencyPerSecond silently misreport for extreme windows with no guard.","confidence":"4/10","evidence":["dora.go: `windowDuration := windowEnd.Sub(windowStart)`, `exactDurationSeconds(windowDuration)`, and `SetFrac(..., big.NewInt(windowDuration.Nanoseconds()))` use the saturated int64 nanosecond count","a probe at 290 years produced a finite WindowSeconds (9145440000) with no error; there is no upper-bound check on the window such as exists for MaximumDurationSec in experiment plans"]}

"Whether the Dinic max-flow recursion (push) can overflow the goroutine stack on deep level graphs for the max allowed problem size (2000 items / 256 resources); not exercised at scale.",
"Whether rounding's reliance on Go map iteration order over flows[item.ID] is fully neutralized by the downstream sort of Fractions; fractions are sorted but any other map-order dependence in round() was not exhaustively ruled out.",
"Whether record-evaluators/assess-evaluators with an empty StoreDirectory is intended to fail closed (Save returns 'twin store directory is required'); behavior observed but not asserted by a committed test."
]}That background task was the pinned-commit test run I already used mid-evaluation: it extracted `b399c05…` to `/tmp/evaltree` and ran `go test ./internal/optimization/... ./cmd/platform-optimizer/...` — both packages passed (`ok`), confirming the committed suite is green before I trusted it as a baseline for the probes.

No follow-up needed. The evaluation is complete and the JSON findings above already account for it. I also removed the temporary probe file from the extracted tree (which lives in `/tmp`, outside the repo), so the repository working tree was never modified.
